outcome: The only in-window event that moves a quantity named in the statement is the diagonal upper bound: Angeltveit and McKay (arXiv:2409.15709, 24 Sep 2024) lowered R(5,5) from 48 to 46 by linear programming plus SAT-based case analysis, while the lower bound 43 (Exoo, 1989) is unchanged and R(5,5) remains undetermined; no AI system is credited with any R(5,5) result, although AI-credited work in 2026 moved lower bounds for other Ramsey numbers (AlphaEvolve: R(3,13), R(3,18), R(4,13) to R(4,20)) and off-diagonal, multicolour and doubly-saturated-graph questions.
problem_asks: (1) The values of the Ramsey numbers, read as the classical two-colour numbers R(r,s) (the least n such that every 2-colouring of the edges of K_n has a red K_r or a blue K_s), i.e. determining R(r,s) for the pairs r,s; the bullet asks for values, so bounds are progress toward it but not a determination. (2) In particular, the exact value of the diagonal number R(5,5), which is known only to satisfy 43 <= R(5,5) <= 46. Scope note: the bare phrase 'the Ramsey numbers' could also reach multicolour, hypergraph and graph-Ramsey numbers; 'particularly R(5,5)' indicates the two-colour classical numbers are the core. Both readings are recorded in the events so the judging pass can apply either.

events.what_happened: Exoo gave a 2-colouring of the edges of K_42 with no monochromatic K_5 (a graph on 42 vertices whose complement is also K_5-free), so R(5,5) >= 43. This is the lower bound still standing in 2026 (cited as best known in arXiv:2409.15709 and in the Wikipedia table). Venue and exact page not opened; the 1989 attribution is from arXiv:2409.15709 and arXiv:2212.12630.
events.delivers: R(5,5) >= 43. Covers the diagonal case only and says nothing about other pairs.
events.remains: The exact value of R(5,5) (open; 43 <= R(5,5) <= 46 as of Oct 2026) and every other R(r,s) value the statement covers.

Not accepted: the R(6,6) half conflicts with the known lower bound R(6,6) >= 102 (Kalbfleisch, 1966), which the Epoch AI page opened for this record states, and the search snippet of the abstract also gives 102 <= R(6,6) <= 165 (abstract not fully read).
events.remains: If the claim were sound it would settle R(5,5) (= 43), but the claim is not accepted, so the R(5,5) value is treated as open in all current sources.

events.doubts: The R(6,6)=91 claim is below the known lower bound R(6,6) >= 102 (Kalbfleisch 1966), which the paper's own abstract (per a search snippet) also states; the abstract (per the fetched copy) describes the method as a partition argument around a vertex with a distance-based colouring condition, and the mathematical argument is not summarised in enough detail to check from the abstract alone.

events.what_happened: Angeltveit and McKay, 'R(5,5) <= 46' (arXiv:2409.15709, v1 24 Sep 2024; v2 1 Sep 2025). They prove R(5,5) <= 46 by combining linear programming with a large computer case analysis. The second version carries no changelog. The computations are SAT-based: the second author uses Glucose with a one-minute limit per problem and Kissat for sanity checks; the first author uses a special-purpose SAT solver for the gluing problems. The paper states that all computations were independently implemented by both authors with consistent results. The paper reports about 15 CPU-years for the census and about 15 for the gluing, so roughly 30 in total, and a replication of about 50 further CPU-years. The lower bound 43 is stated to be still the best. Blog coverage (Gasarch, 29 Sep 2024) summarises the result and adds that Glucose was used; it does not check the argument.
events.revisions: v1 24 Sep 2024; v2 1 Sep 2025 (no changelog visible)
events.delivers: R(5,5) <= 46 (diagonal, all parameters). This is a single upper bound and it moves the diagonal upper bound from 48 to 46; the lower bound stays at 43. It is a full result for the diagonal case, not restricted to a range.
events.remains: The exact value of R(5,5), which lies in {43, 44, 45, 46}. Every other pair named by the statement is untouched.
events.time_since_posted: about 2 years (as of 13 Oct 2026); no journal version and no external re-verification found in searches

machine_checked.system: SAT solvers Glucose (main) and Kissat (sanity), a special-purpose SAT solver (first author), and linear programming; computations independently implemented by both authors

events.directly_checkable: Not by hand: the proof is a finite computer case analysis (about 12 million (G,H)-overlaps; 5.6 million processed by Glucose; 8,485,247 graphs in R(5,5,37) with none extending to R(5,5,38), per Sections 6-7 of v2). Checking requires re-running the pipeline.
events.direction: Upper bound R(5,5) <= 46: moves the diagonal bound toward the conjectured 43 but does not decide the value. It cuts neither for nor against 43 beyond what the bounds state.

events.what_happened: Tamburini, 'Random-projector quantum diagnostics of Ramsey numbers and a prime-factor heuristic for R(5,5)=45' (arXiv:2508.16699, v1 22 Aug 2025; v2 11 Sep 2025). Embeds two-colour Ramsey instances into a graded Majorana algebra, uses randomised spectral diagnostics in place of enumeration, reports that both diagnostics 'identify R(5,5) at n=45', and proposes a prime-sequence consistency heuristic. The paper presents this as a heuristic, not a proof.
events.delivers: A heuristic claim that R(5,5) = 45. No proof and no explicit colouring; it establishes no bound.
events.remains: Everything in the statement; the claim is heuristic and not an established value.
events.doubts: The value 45 is a heuristic output of randomised spectral diagnostics (title and abstract say so); the paper gives no explicit colouring or proof, and the 2026 CMU study and the widely cited conjecture R(5,5)=43 point elsewhere, so the claim is in tension with the cited conjecture.
events.direction: Asserts R(5,5)=45 heuristically, against the widely cited conjectured value 43; it proves nothing.

events.what_happened: Nagda, Raghavan and Guha Thakurta, 'Reinforced Generation of Combinatorial Structures: Ramsey Numbers' (arXiv:2603.09172, a working paper). Using AlphaEvolve, described as 'an LLM-based code mutation agent', they report improved lower bounds for classical two-colour Ramsey numbers. The v1 (10 Mar 2026) reports five: R(3,13) 60 to 61, R(3,18) 99 to 100, R(4,13) 138 to 139, R(4,14) 147 to 148, R(4,15) 158 to 159. The v5 (21 Apr 2026) reports nine, adding R(4,16) 170 to 174, R(4,18) 205 to 209, R(4,19) 213 to 219 and R(4,20) 234 to 237. The paper says 28 bounds are matched or improved and that it recovers all exactly known values. R(5,5) is not among the improved entries; the v5 table lists R(5,7), R(5,8), R(5,9) only (their status is not readable from the extracted text).
events.revisions: v1 10 Mar 2026; v2 11 Mar 2026; v3 9 Apr 2026; v4 11 Apr 2026; v5 21 Apr 2026. The count of improved bounds changed from five (v1) to nine (v5); no changelog on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Lower bounds for R(3,13), R(3,18), R(4,13), R(4,14), R(4,15), and in v5 also R(4,16), R(4,18), R(4,19), R(4,20). Only the listed pairs. Nothing for R(5,5); R(5,k) appears only for k = 7, 8, 9 in the table.
events.remains: The exact values of the listed pairs (still open), R(5,5), and all other pairs.
events.time_since_posted: about 7 months; described by the authors as a working paper, not peer reviewed
events.directly_checkable: Each witness graph (on 60, 99, 138, 147, 158 vertices for v1; on 173, 208, 218, 236 vertices added in v5) can be checked by computer for the absence of red K_r and blue K_s. The authors state the search code is on GitHub (google-research repository, ramsey_number_bounds/improved_bounds); the repository was not opened.
events.doubts: The count of improved bounds changes between versions (five in v1, nine in v5) with no changelog, which is a scope change between versions. The paper says the final graphs are checked only by the algorithm's own tests (a keep-condition on cliques and independent sets, and an exact solver in one case); no independent check is described. The authors also state that AlphaEvolve 'quoted the corresponding adjacency matrices from the LLM's memory' for R(3,3) and R(3,4), which they left out, so LLM recall is part of their pipeline.
events.direction: Lower bounds only, moving the listed pairs up; no bearing on R(5,5), and no move toward or away from the conjectured 43 for the diagonal.
events.object: Witness graphs for each improved pair: a graph on n-1 vertices with no red K_r and no blue K_s, where n is the new bound (for example a graph on 60 vertices witnessing R(3,13) >= 61). Explicit search outputs, not non-constructive existence proofs. Their construction is described as evolved stochastic search algorithms; the human effort is said to be in the overarching Algorithm 1.

events.what_happened: Przybocki, Mackey, Heule and Subercaseaux, 'Doubly Saturated Ramsey Graphs: A Case Study in Computer-Assisted Mathematical Discovery' (arXiv:2604.21187, 23 Apr 2026, v1 only). They study Ramsey-good graphs (no s-clique and no t-independent set) that are doubly saturated (adding or deleting any edge creates an s-clique or t-independent set), answering a 1982 question of Grinstead and Roberts with infinite families. The method combines SAT solving with LLM-generated code, and LLMs generate proofs that are formalised in Lean. In their own words the discovery was almost entirely LLM-driven.

The paper uses R(s,t) as shorthand for a graph property and does not give classical values. Not a value of any R(r,s); nothing about R(5,5), which it mentions only in a quotation of the Angeltveit-McKay bound.

events.what_happened: Bradac, 'Off-diagonal Ramsey numbers' (arXiv:2605.28793): the current version (v3, 16 Jun 2026) proves, for fixed s >= 3 and k tending to infinity, r(s,k) >= k^(s-1) / (log k)^(2s-4), matching the Erdos-Szekeres upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors, and improving Spencer's 1977 bound for s >= 5. The exponent s-1 appears in the current version; v2 (11 Jun 2026) was not checked, so the first version carrying s-1 may be v2 or v3. The Erdos Problems forum (thread 986) says the problem 'was proved by Bradac', and says the adjustment to s-1 'was observed by an internal model at OpenAI' (page text, not a forum post). The arXiv abstract page does not mention OpenAI or AI. Scientific American reports the same attribution (search summary, not opened).
events.revisions: v1 27 May 2026 (s-2); v2 11 Jun 2026 (not checked); v3 16 Jun 2026 (s-1, current)
events.delivers: Lower bound r(s,k) >= k^(s-1) / (log k)^(2s-4) for fixed s >= 3, k to infinity; off-diagonal and asymptotic. Matches the Erdos-Szekeres upper bound up to polylogs, so the remaining gap is polylogarithmic in the lower bound. Not the diagonal R(5,5) and not an exact value.
events.remains: Exact values of r(s,k) and R(5,5); the polylogarithmic gap.

disputes.summary: Lee (JKSCI, 2015) claims R(5,5)=43 and R(6,6)=91. The R(6,6) value conflicts with the known lower bound R(6,6) >= 102 (Kalbfleisch 1966), and no literature accepts the claim; the current sources all keep R(5,5) open at 43 to 46.

The triangle multicolour result: Steiner's note says 'OpenAI proved' the super-exponential bound and credits the odd-cycle extension to ChatGPT 5.6 Pro/Sol; an IBS seminar listing says 'OpenAI, using an internal AI model'. No OpenAI primary source was found, so the model that produced the original construction is unresolved.

Bradac's s-1 exponent: the Erdos forum page (thread 986) says it 'was observed by an internal model at OpenAI'; the authors' arXiv abstract page does not mention OpenAI or AI. No authors' own account of AI involvement was found, so the AI claim is unsupported by the authors.

AlphaEvolve Ramsey paper: v1 reports five improved lower bounds, v5 reports nine (adds R(4,16), R(4,18), R(4,19), R(4,20)); there is no changelog, so the change in scope between versions is unexplained.

summary: The problem asks for the values of the Ramsey numbers, particularly R(5,5). Known bounds at the time of this search (13 Oct 2026): 43 <= R(5,5) <= 46. The lower bound 43 is Exoo's 1989 construction and has not moved. The upper bound moved from 48 (Angeltveit and McKay, 2017) to 46 in an in-window preprint by Angeltveit and McKay (arXiv:2409.15709, 24 Sep 2024; v2 1 Sep 2025, no changelog). That proof is a finite computer case analysis using linear programming and SAT solvers (Glucose and Kissat, per the v2 full text), with each computation independently implemented by both authors. I found no independent re-verification and no journal version. A blog post (Gasarch, 29 Sep 2024) summarises it without checking it, and the Wikipedia 'Ramsey's theorem' table (opened) gives 43 to 46 for R(5,5), 40 to 41 for R(3,10) and 36 to 40 for R(4,6). Other in-window events that touch R(5,5) do not move the bounds: a heuristic claim R(5,5)=45 (Tamburini, Aug 2025, no proof); a Carnegie Mellon SAT study (March 2026 talk) that excludes 141 of 313 symmetry-reduced cases of a hypothetical strongly regular graph which would give R(5,5)=46, with the remaining 172 unreported. Searches for any 2026 claim on R(5,5) itself (including AI-credited claims) found none; the Epoch AI open-problem page for R(6,6) lists R(5,5) as open and names no AI attempt. AI-involved work does exist in the wider family of Ramsey numbers. AlphaEvolve (Nagda, Raghavan and Guha Thakurta, arXiv:2603.09172, Mar to Apr 2026) improved lower bounds for R(3,13), R(3,18) and R(4,13) to R(4,20) (nine in v5); its v5 table lists R(5,7), R(5,8), R(5,9) and no R(5,5). The authors credit AlphaEvolve, an LLM-based code mutation agent, with the search procedures that give these constructions, and say Gemini 3 was used to summarise the evolved code and build a classification table (not load-bearing; recorded here and not put in ai.systems). Przybocki, Mackey, Heule and Subercaseaux (arXiv:2604.21187, 23 Apr 2026) credit ChatGPT, Gemini and ChatGPT-5.4 Pro with the conjecture and proof of results on doubly saturated Ramsey-good graphs, a different question. Steiner (arXiv:2608.02537, Aug 2026) credits ChatGPT 5.6 Pro/Sol with the autonomous proof of an odd-cycle multicolour extension, and the same month OpenAI is reported (secondary sources only) to have proved a super-exponential multicolour triangle bound. Bradac's off-diagonal result (v3 16 Jun 2026, exponent s-1) is attributed to an OpenAI internal model only by a forum page and press, not by the authors. A pre-window claim, Lee (2015), that R(5,5)=43 and R(6,6)=91 is unaccepted and conflicts with R(6,6) >= 102. The pre-window R(3,10) <= 41 (Angeltveit, arXiv 31 Dec 2023, EJC 2025) is a genuine two-colour value bound; it is recorded as predating the frozen revision and does not touch R(5,5). Where a call was close: (a) whether 'the Ramsey numbers' includes the off-diagonal, multicolour and asymptotic families, which the statement's wording allows but 'particularly R(5,5)' does not require; (b) whether an AlphaEvolve lower bound for R(3,13) or R(4,20) is progress on 'the values' when R(5,5) is untouched; (c) whether the Bradac and triangle attributions to OpenAI count as AI involvement without the authors' own statement. My reading: the only event that moves a quantity named in the two-colour, diagonal reading of the statement is the in-window, non-AI 2024 upper bound.
competing_reading: Read broadly, 'the values of the Ramsey numbers' covers every R(r,s) and every multicolour and asymptotic family, so in-window progress includes AlphaEvolve's lower bounds for R(3,13), R(3,18) and R(4,13) to R(4,20) (March-April 2026, AI-credited), Coniglio et al.'s R(3,n) lower bounds (August 2026, not AI), the CJMS, Hefty et al. and Gupta et al. asymptotics, and the AI-credited multicolour and off-diagonal results. On that reading the problem has moved a great deal and AI is involved in several of the moves. Read narrowly, 'particularly R(5,5)' fixes the problem to the diagonal two-colour value, where only the 2024 upper bound moved, and no AI system is involved.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The 24 Apr 2026 version of Radziszowski's dynamic survey DS1 (the landing page was read; its PDF was unreadable to the fetcher), whose R(5,5) and other table entries would confirm that no later R(5,5) change is recorded. (2) A check of arXiv math.CO for R(5,5) and for any Angeltveit or McKay preprint after September 2025. (3) A replication or verification of the 46 bound, or its journal publication. (4) The full text of the Braginsky et al. talk for the outcome of the 172 remaining SAT subcases. (5) OpenAI's own write-up of the triangle result and of the Bradac s-1 step, and the authors' own text on which tool, if any, produced them. (6) For AlphaEvolve, the status entries of R(5,7), R(5,8), R(5,9) in the v5 table, and the GitHub code. (7) For Trellis (arXiv:2606.09674), the repository and whether it contains sorry. (8) Whether the Lee (2015) paper ever drew a response.
